claims.text: Phase evolution in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs can be precisely controlled by tailoring thermal history.
Cooling rate is an effective control parameter for phase evolution in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs.
Annealing temperature is an effective control parameter for phase evolution in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs.
Rapid solidification produces a non-equilibrium Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEA with an initially homogeneous microstructure.
In-situ X-ray diffraction and differential scanning calorimetry can be used to monitor the phase transformations during controlled thermal cycling.
A controlled atmosphere limits oxidation effects during the proposed thermal treatments.
Annealing treatment can drive evolution between ordered B2 and disordered BCC phases in the Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni system.
The distribution and length scale of B2+BCC decomposition depend on annealing temperature.
Diffusion kinetics and thermodynamic equilibrium mediate the thermally induced evolution of B2 and BCC phases.
Changing cooling rate and annealing temperature changes the nucleation and growth kinetics of phase transformations.
These kinetic changes dictate the size, morphology, and fraction of equilibrium and metastable phases.
Systematic variation of thermal treatment will produce reproducible and tunable differences in phase fractions.
Thermal treatment can select between a two-phase B2+BCC microstructure and a metastable single-phase microstructure.
Differences in B2+BCC phase constitution and decomposition length scale can be correlated with altered mechanical properties.
Rapid quenching typically produces a metastable single-phase Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni microstructure.
Thermal-history control is effective only within a defined range of cooling rates and annealing temperatures.
Treatments outside the effective range may cause incomplete phase transformation or undesirable coarsening.
Grain growth or secondary-phase precipitation may compete with the proposed phase evolution and introduce variability.
